This study presents a novel time-varying Bayesian autoregression model, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our model, called TVPAR, accounts for both structural changes in the model's parameters over time and nonlinear relationships between past values and the current count. We develop an efficient Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulation framework to estimate TVPAR's parameters, taking into consideration the non-linear relationships and varying components. Furthermore, we derive an empirical Bayes estimate for the nonlinear parts of the model to streamline the MCMC process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TVPAR through a simulation study and also apply it to real-world data sets, showcasing its ability to accurately forecast counts and identify nonlinear patterns. We have made the TVPAR code publicly available to facilitate its use by others. Its potential applications extend to analyzing count-based time series data in various domains, including economics, public health, and sports analytics. Its ability to handle nonlinear relationships and varying parameters makes it particularly suitable for analyzing data with complex dynamics and trends. (2 pages)

Deep learning models continue to experience significant growth in size and complexity, making efficient use of computational resources more crucial than ever. Previously published works on reducing CPU frequencies for energy efficiency were mainly focused on low-power edge devices and NLP tasks like language models. However, our research targets a broader scope of tasks, including computer vision models and general-purpose computing, demonstrating the potential to further decrease CPU frequencies beyond what was previously achievable. Through a combination of performance throttling and dynamic voltage and frequency scaling, we successfully reduced the operating frequency of a GHz-range CPU to a range of 2.4 to 3.2 MHz, resulting in significant energy savings of up to 13.5 times with minimal impact on performance, measured as a 1.5 times increase in latency and a 50% decrease in accuracy for certain tasks. Our optimized operating frequency range was achieved with a ResNet-50 model on ImageNet, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach on real-world data. Our findings provide valuable insights for hardware designers on the feasibility of creating ultra-low power CPUs and offer a versatile performance spectrum for developers to balance performance and energy efficiency in their applications. Our research is available under an open-source license, contributing to the creation of a low-power deep learning computing stack. A pre-compiled ResNet-50 model trained on ImageNet is also provided to facilitate evaluation. The code and models can be found at https://github.com/ghloogh/HyperDegrade.

Deep learning models for classification tasks are often evaluated and trained using accurate classification loss functions like cross-entropy. However, in real-world scenarios with imperfect data, particularly in medical diagnostics, a misclassified instance might have little practical significance. A low birth rate or a need for additional training on such instances could hinder the development of effective models. To address this, we explore the potential benefits of using loss functions that weigh the importance of different classification errors, aligning with the true risk a model will face in real-world applications. By analyzing both theoretical expectations and real-world data from a diabetes diagnosis dataset, we determine whether such weighted loss functions lead to better performance in medical diagnostic tasks and draw a distinction between their capabilities and the influence of regularization. Our findings indicate that in medical diagnostic tasks, using a weighted loss function does not necessarily result in better performance when the classes are balanced, but it can lead to improved performance when the classes are imbalanced, as it prioritizes the accurate classification of more common conditions. Furthermore, we observe that the incorporation of extra weights does not necessarily translate to improved performance on rare conditions, and in some cases may even degrade it. To conclude, we advise using a constant weighted loss function, such as the balanced cross-entropy loss, as it strikes a fair balance between different classification errors by weighting the true risks a model will face in real-world applications. Additionally, we find that the use of weighted loss functions does not necessarily require the use of dropout regularization, as it can be viewed as a form of regularization that reduces the true risk of overfitting on rare classes, similar to L1 or L2 regularization. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording setups.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective techniques to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been recorded in noisy environments using unconventional microphones and under varying acoustic conditions.  Techniques are proposed to process heart sounds that have been affected by smearing, a common issue with optical stethoscopes, and a new method is introduced to remove non-linear distortions.  To tackle these challenges, a new dataset was created consisting of sounds recorded with a high-speed camera-based stethoscope and a conventional electronic stethoscope in noisy backgrounds and quiet environments.  To differentiate normal and abnormal heart sounds, an experiment was conducted using the created dataset in combination with widely used datasets from previous studies.  The results showed that the newly created techniques outperformed existing methods when evaluating the effectiveness of heart sound analysis techniques. We create two new parameters: a line width corrected for non-thermal broadening and a gas mass estimate that considers subthermal effects. Utilizing a sample of 30 local galaxies with both C I and C II data, we explore the consequences of incorporating these new measures. The corrected line width shows improved agreement with molecular gas fractions observed in sound waves, while the subthermally corrected gas mass shows enhanced correlation with thermal gas pressures. These new definitions particularly highlight the significance of C I (2-1, 5-4) in measuring massive, star-forming gas reservoirs, even in low signal-to-noise data. Furthermore, this new perspective may prove valuable in using C I lines to study both present and past gas behavior in various astronomical contexts. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the potential utility of C I line measurements in exploring the dynamics and physical conditions of molecular gas within galaxies. This study conducts a sentiment classification task on low-resource Hindi news articles, using a combination of high-resource English data and bridge languages, specifically German and Russian. A multi-task learning approach is employed, where the system is trained on multiple tasks: Hindi, English, and the bridge languages, with the intention of leveraging existing English resources. A German-based pipeline and a Russian-based pipeline are compared, using three settings: individual tasks, combined tasks, and combined tasks with shared hidden layers. The results show that the most effective setup uses the German-based pipeline with the combined English and German tasks. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. The resulting dataset is highly valuable for developing and evaluating models that predict discourse indicators between sentences, as well as models that carry out discourse relation identification within sentences.
